title: Delilah, Blindness, and the Fall of Dagon's Temple
summary: Samson escapes an ambush at Gaza by carrying off the city gate. He falls in love with Delilah, who is paid by the Philistine lords to discover the secret of his strength; after three false answers he tells her the truth, his hair is shaved, and the LORD leaves him. Blinded and imprisoned, Samson is brought out to entertain the Philistines at a festival to Dagon, prays for strength once more, and pulls down the temple, killing more in his death than in his life.
story: This is the end of Samson's story and the last account of a judge in the book. The chapter follows the pattern of the earlier ones (a woman, a secret, betrayal, and violence), but now the cost falls on Samson himself. His consecration, already neglected, is finally broken, and the Spirit who had rushed upon him departs without his noticing. The Philistines celebrate, crediting their god Dagon with his capture, which turns the story into a contest between the LORD and Dagon. The judge who was to begin Israel's deliverance ends as a blind prisoner, yet his final prayer is answered. After this, Judges shows no more deliverers, only the collapse of chapters 17-21.
historical:
Gaza was the southernmost of the five Philistine cities, near the Mediterranean coast. Hebron lay in the hill country of Judah, roughly forty miles to the east and some three thousand feet higher. Whether Samson carried the gates all that way or to a hill facing Hebron is debated, but either way the feat is enormous and the humiliation for Gaza great. The Valley of Sorek, home of Delilah, is the same valley that runs past Zorah, Eshtaol, and Timnah. The text doesn't say whether Delilah was a Philistine or an Israelite.

Dagon was an ancient Semitic god, worshiped in Syria and Mesopotamia long before the Philistines arrived; texts from Ebla and Mari mention him. The Philistines adopted him, and he had temples in Gaza and Ashdod (1 Samuel 5:1-5). The older idea that Dagon was a fish-god is now generally doubted; his name is related to a Semitic word for grain, and many scholars think he was associated with grain or storms. Excavations at Tell Qasile, a Philistine site near modern Tel Aviv, have uncovered a temple from this period whose roof rested on two central wooden pillars set on stone bases, which helps a reader picture the scene in 16:29.
cultural:
The bribe offered to Delilah was huge. Each lord of the Philistines promised eleven hundred shekels of silver; with five lords, the total was about five thousand five hundred shekels. By comparison, the Levite in 17:10 is offered ten shekels a year. Weapons and methods of binding (fresh bowstrings, new ropes, weaving hair into a loom) were drawn from daily life. Women commonly wove cloth on looms at home, and Delilah's loom would have been an ordinary household object.

Blinding prisoners and forcing them to grind grain were known practices in the ancient Near East. Grinding at a mill was hard, menial work normally done by women and slaves; for a war hero it was a deliberate humiliation. Victories were credited to the gods of the victorious people, which is why the Philistines praise Dagon for delivering Samson into their hands. A festival with sacrifice, feasting, and entertainment was an ordinary occasion for public celebration of a god.
literary: The chapter is built on a threefold pattern followed by a fourth, decisive act. Three times Delilah asks, Samson lies, she binds him, calls out that the Philistines are here, and he breaks free. Each lie comes closer to the truth: the third involves his hair. The fourth time he tells her all that is in his heart, a phrase repeated three times in 16:17-18. The narrator then uses a devastating understatement: Samson thought he would shake himself free as before, but he did not know that the LORD had departed from him (16:20). The quiet note that his hair began to grow again (16:22) signals hope. The chapter closes with a reversal: the Philistine song celebrates Samson's capture, and Samson's final prayer, “O Lord GOD, please remember me” (16:28), leads to their destruction. The final verse brings his story to rest in his father's tomb.

Three attempts to learn the secret of his strength
Samson reveals his secret, is shaved, blinded, and imprisoned
Samson's prayer, the temple's fall, and his burial

doctrines.note: Samson's strength was tied to his consecration to God. When the last visible sign of that consecration was removed, the LORD departed. Holiness is not magic in the hair but a relationship of belonging to God, which Samson had long neglected.
Samson's final prayer asks God to remember him and strengthen him once more. Even at the end of a life of self-will, God hears, which shows the reach of grace.

The Philistines credit Dagon with Samson's capture, and the temple of Dagon becomes the place of their defeat. The story shows the LORD triumphing over the gods of the nations, a theme continued when Dagon's statue falls before the ark in 1 Samuel 5.

words.note: Koach, strength or power, used seven times in the chapter. Delilah's question is always about the source of his great strength. The answer is not ultimately his hair but the LORD, whose departure leaves Samson as weak as any man. Samson's final prayer asks God to strengthen him, recognizing where his power came from.

Sur, to turn aside or depart. In 16:17 Samson says his strength will depart; in 16:19 it does; and in 16:20 the LORD departs from him. The same verb covers the loss of strength and the loss of God's presence, tying the two together. The saddest line in the story is that Samson did not know.

Dagon, the chief god of the Philistines. His name probably relates to a Semitic word for grain. The festival in his honor becomes the scene of the LORD's victory, and the story sets up the larger contest between the LORD and Dagon in 1 Samuel 5.

Zakhar, to remember. When Samson asks God to remember him (16:28), he is asking not for mere recollection but for God to act on his behalf. In the Old Testament, God's remembering his people, as he remembered Noah, Abraham, and Rachel, leads to his intervention.

christ: Samson's death has often been compared with Christ's, and the New Testament includes Samson among those who acted by faith (Hebrews 11:32). The comparison is thematic and works mainly through contrast. Samson was betrayed for silver by someone close to him, handed over to his enemies, mocked, and killed, and in his death he struck a decisive blow against Israel's enemies. Jesus was also betrayed for silver, mocked, and killed, and by his death he triumphed over the powers of evil (Colossians 2:15). But Samson's death was an act of vengeance for his two eyes, and he died with his enemies; Jesus died forgiving his enemies and rose again to give them life. Samson shows what a flawed deliverer can do. Jesus shows what a faithful one does. The longing for a deliverer who is both powerful and faithful is one of the threads Judges leaves for later books to take up.

hard.q: Was Samson's final act a suicide, and how could God answer a prayer for revenge?
hard.a: The question has been debated for centuries. Some interpreters, including Augustine in The City of God, argued that Samson's death was not a sinful suicide because he acted by a special prompting of God, shown by God's answer to his prayer. Others see his act as a warrior's death in battle, taking enemies with him, rather than a suicide in the modern sense. Still others think Samson's motive was mixed at best, since he asked to pay back the Philistines for his two eyes, and that God answered his prayer because of his larger purpose for Israel, not because the motive was pure. The narrator gives no verdict on Samson's intention, but the answered prayer shows that God had not finished with him. The chapter holds together Samson's failure, God's patience, and God's victory over Dagon.

questions: Samson did not know that the LORD had left him. How can someone drift so gradually from God that they do not notice what they have lost?
Delilah pressed Samson day after day until he told her everything. Where are you vulnerable to pressure that wears you down over time?
Samson's hair began to grow again, and his last prayer was answered. What does his story say about the possibility of grace after failure?
